name: Reddish Brown
lede: Reddish brown is a description that became a color name: a dark, strong brown tilted toward red, found in mineral lists, pigment catalogues and painters' grounds long before it was a swatch.

sections.title: A description before a name
sections.body:
*Reddish brown* is a phrase before it is a color name. The color lists in the Werner tradition, from the 1790s, already carry *reddish-brown* beside clove brown, liver brown and tombac brown [1]. An English treatise on diamonds and precious stones used the term in 1813, for tourmalines [1].

Our swatch, a dark and strongly colored reddish brown, comes from ISCC-NBS block 46 and the xkcd color survey [2]. Its nearest named neighbor on our chart is [[mahogany]], 6.8 units away [2]. No single material makes this color, which is why dictionaries lean on the phrase to define so many others.

sections.title: The word dictionaries lean on
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary uses *reddish-brown* to pin down whole families of older names. Acajou is the reddish-brown of mahogany, argil is the reddish-brown of potter's clay, and bay is the reddish brown of a horse's coat [3]. [[bole]] is an orange-red or reddish-brown earth pigment, and amadou brown and autumn brown are darker and warmer versions [3].

[[burnt-umber]] is the standard pigment case. Roasting raw [[umber]] in air dehydrates its iron hydroxides into iron oxides, and the result is a warm reddish brown that keeps raw umber's power as a drier [3][4].

The phrase also covers organic colorants. Annatto and cochineal were common reddish-brown colorants in Mexican manuscript painting in the sixteenth century and before [4]. The ink of the cuttlefish owes its color to two melanins, the black eumelanins and the reddish-brown pheomelanins [4]. That is the chemistry behind [[sepia]].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
Ball reports that Tintoretto sought tonal unity with dark reddish-brown grounds, deeper than the ones under Leonardo's sfumato [5]. Caravaggio used the same technique to wrap his scenes in shadow [5]. Rembrandt used bitumen, a tarry brown, in reddish-brown glazes without mishap, but it never dries properly, and in Reynolds's hands it was a disaster [5].

A varnish can also make a painting reddish brown. Until the 1970s, [[painter:peter-paul-rubens|Rubens]]'s *Gerbier Family* in Washington lay under a toned nineteenth-century varnish, and the critic Roger Fry saw in it a harmony of coppery reds and reddish browns with a nearly neutral grey [6]. Removing the varnish changed the greys to blues and the reds to greens [6].

Outside studios the term turns up at turning points. Perkin's first try at synthetic quinine in 1856 left a reddish-brown sludge, and the next experiment gave [[mauve]] [7]. Le Corbusier's account of the Parthenon went muted and ochre, the marble seeming as reddish-brown as terra-cotta before a storm whitened the hill [8].

sections.title: On skin and cloth
sections.body: Egyptian funerary painting gave men red or reddish-brown complexions, and women lighter beige or yellowish ones [9]. Henna, a bush of warm regions, gives a dye of red or reddish brown when its leaves are dried and powdered, used on cloth, leather, wood, hair, nails and skin [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a common painted color. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 683 works, 2.9 per cent of the archive [10]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color and not a pigment test [10].

Its peak is early: 68 of 945 paintings from the 1400s carry it (7.2 per cent, 2.5 times the archive rate), and the single best decade is the 1430s, with 6 of 51 [10]. It falls away to 14 of 1,674 paintings from the 1900s [10]. The painters who use it most, among those with enough dated works, include Batoni (4 of 13 paintings), Modigliani (4 of 18) and [[painter:peter-paul-rubens|Rubens]] (7 of 46) [10]. Inside a painting it is a mid-tone in 81 per cent of cases [10].

The largest patches are in a [[painting:commons-Q21723078|portrait of Otto Buchholtz]] (1830, 40 per cent of the canvas), van de Venne's [[painting:rijks-200108366|Prince Maurits on his deathbed]] (1625, 40 per cent) and Titian's [[painting:nga-41638|Cardinal Pietro Bembo]] (1539, 34 per cent) [10]. The earliest dated match is a [[painting:aic-14968|mural fragment]] of a maguey bloodletting ritual, about 500, at 12 per cent [10]. The color keeps company with [[maroon]], [[rust]], [[brick]] and [[chocolate]] [10]. In Google Books the phrase *reddish brown* peaks around 1925 [11].

choices: Greys turned to blues and reds to greens
questions.answer: Greys turned to blues and reds to greens

questions.q: True or false: bitumen, which Rembrandt used in reddish-brown glazes, dries well in thick films.
In which century is this reddish brown most over-represented in our painting archive?

Look for this color in the 1400s: it is 2.5 times as common there as in the archive as a whole.
